title: “Glassmorphism in user interfaces”
lede: The November 2020 essay that gave the style its name and listed its four defining traits.
summary: Michał Malewicz names glassmorphism: background blur, floating layers, vivid color, and a light border.

evidence.note: Inspected the article’s header image (1750 × 962, from Medium’s CDN) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The UX Collective copy is member-only and returns HTTP 403 to scripts; its preview and date were read in Claude in Chrome. The full text was read from the Wayback capture of the Hype4 Academy copy (19 January 2022), which includes a “2021 Update” section.

styles.note: The naming text of the style. Its header illustration is itself a textbook example: frosted cards with light edges over a cyan-to-magenta gradient.

context: Malewicz lists the style’s “most defining characteristics”: transparency (a frosted-glass effect through background blur), a multi-layered approach with objects floating in space, vivid colors that highlight the blurred transparency, and a subtle light border on the translucent objects. He writes that “the best way to call it is GLASSMORPHISM”. [Hype4 Academy copy, Wayback 2022](https://web.archive.org/web/20220119095027/https://hype4.academy/articles/design/glassmorphism-in-user-interfaces).

He traces background blur to iOS 7 (2013), notes its return in macOS Big Sur, and quotes Microsoft’s definition of Fluent [Acrylic](ref:microsoft-fluent-acrylic-material). He cites Dribbble examples, among them the [Smart Calendar App](ref:paperpillar-smart-calendar-app-2020) by Ghani Pradita.

Practical advice in the text: make only the fill transparent, not the whole object, or design tools drop the background blur; choose a background with enough tonal difference; add a 1 pt semi-transparent inner border to simulate the glass edge; keep buttons and toggles opaque for contrast.

The article follows his 2019 neumorphism essay and says that neumorphism imitated an extruded plastic surface in one layer, while the new style “goes a bit more vertical”. The generator on [Hype4 Academy](ref:hype4-glassmorphism-generator) calls this piece “the original article that named the trend”.
observed: A saturated background runs from cyan at the top corners through violet to hot pink at the bottom.
A central phone-shaped panel and several credit cards are milky, semi-transparent white. The gradient shows through them as soft pink and blue.
Every card has large rounded corners and a thin, lighter edge. Round icon buttons (a star, a bell, a cart) sit in translucent discs with a light rim.
The front card is almost opaque white; the side cards are more transparent. The primary button (“RENEW”) is a solid white pill.
Huge white letters spelling GLASSMORPHISM sit behind the cards and blur where the cards overlap them.
interpretation: The header image shows the full recipe at once, including hierarchy through opacity: the most important card is the least transparent. Malewicz calls the example “purposefully over the top”.
borrow: Signal hierarchy with opacity: make the front card nearly opaque and let the cards behind it be more transparent.
Put large type behind the glass so that the blur is visible even over a simple gradient.
